blocks.text: The chapter moves from Jesus’ Spirit-led testing in the wilderness to the beginning of his public work in Galilee. The first movement presents his sonship through a contest shaped by Scripture. The second joins his call to repentance and announcement of the approaching kingdom with the calling of fishermen, teaching, proclamation, healing, and exorcism.

Matthew uses Scripture in two prominent ways here. During the wilderness testing, both the devil and Jesus quote it, but Jesus’ answers repeatedly draw on Deuteronomy to interpret faithful sonship. Later, Matthew introduces the move to Capernaum with a fulfillment formula and Isaiah’s language of light rising in darkness. Scripture therefore appears not merely as an occasional quotation but as a recurring voice through which Matthew frames the events he narrates. The precise scriptural forms behind Matthew’s citations are a matter of interpretation because his Gospel draws on varied Hebrew and Greek forms.

The Galilee of this chapter belonged to the Early Roman world and was governed during most of Jesus’ ministry by Herod Antipas rather than by the Roman prefect of Judea. Its villages combined farming, fishing, crafts, markets, and movement along lake and land routes. Jewish household, synagogue, purity, festival, and subsistence practices substantially shaped the region, though local communities varied and also participated in wider exchange. This keeps Galilee from being imagined either as isolated from Jewish life or as simply reproducing Jerusalem’s institutions.

Capernaum was a Jewish settlement beside the lake in the territory of Herod Antipas, situated within Galilee’s lake economy and near regional routes. Archaeology describes an Early Roman village of basalt-built domestic compounds. Gospel episodes associated with the settlement place homes, hospitality, communal reputation, Sabbath assembly, and healing in the same village setting. The monumental synagogue known from a later period should not be projected backward as the building standing during Jesus’ ministry.

The calling scene is rooted in both work and family. Simon and Andrew are brothers working with nets, while James and John work in a boat with their father Zebedee. Their world was shaped by family networks, vocation, kinship obligations, and household economy. Matthew’s details about leaving nets, boat, and father therefore locate their response within the ordinary structures by which work and family life were organized.

Jesus’ public proclamation begins with repentance because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. The closing summary broadens the picture: he teaches in synagogues, proclaims the good news of the kingdom, heals diseases and sicknesses, and receives people described through several categories of bodily suffering and spiritual affliction. Matthew thus presents his public activity in several registers at once—teaching, proclamation, healing, and exorcism—within ancient ways of speaking about bodies and spirits.
